extracted.intended_audience: middle/high-school drama students enrolled in Caitlin's stand-up comedy unit
extracted.subtask_description: A classroom unit plan for developing observational stand-up comedy, guiding students from generating material through rehearsal and performance assessment, with classroom procedures and journaling requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10-minute performance goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The challenge is to develop 10 minutes of stand-up comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unit-level product goal: students work toward producing a 10-minute set as the culminating performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Question — Generating material
rubrics_metrics.description: How do we start to generate our own material?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rotate depending on where you are in class; instructor will guide students through idea-generation processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Question — Delivery and laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: How does delivery of material help to get laughs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the relationship between comedic delivery and audience response; informs revision and coaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Question — Using feedback to revise
rubrics_metrics.description: How do we use feedback from the audience and ourselves to revise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes iterative improvement based on audience/self-reflection and coach feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Question — Personal style / point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: What is your personal style of observation- what is your Point of View?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are expected to identify and develop a personal POV as part of their comedic identity and material choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Question — Idea to performance (creative process)
rubrics_metrics.description: How do we go from 'idea' to 'performance?' What is our 'creative process?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses students' ability to move material through drafting, testing, revision, and rehearsal into a performed bit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy Journal — record written brainstorms
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to record your written brainstorm in your COMEDY JOURNAL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provided template to structure your journal; try multiple brainstorming methods (Letter of Hate, The Seven Deadly Sins, Multiple Choice Test, etc.). Instructor will check the comedy journal for assessment. Emphasis on quantity: 'Good, bad, funny, not funny- it doesn't matter but the MORE THE BETTER.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Asynchronous material generation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for rotating between written material and material generated from games across days (e.g., Day 1: Letter of Hate; Day 2: pattern game; Day 3: watch video and pull funny bits; Day 4–5: Share Days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the day-by-day rotation to accumulate material and use coach check-ins to stay on track.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating material — out loud testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Grab a partner or two. Share written material out loud with them—note their reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anything sticks out as interesting or funny, highlight or circle it. If you have none, play games and record them. Share work in the COMEDY JOURNAL; you can embed video clips or transcribe material you want to keep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing your first bit — use resources and coaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you start—watch the provided video for inspiration and read the guide; then come coach with Caitlin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the guide, try writing the bit, then seek coach feedback to refine structure and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video assessment — submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit a video assessment at least once a week following the specified procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: 1) Note in your journal when you took the video so there is a record. 2) Submit your video to [email protected] with the subject line: VIDEO ASSESSMENT and the name of your group. 3) Each video assessment will be added to your evidence for COMMUNICATE. After submission, watch your video back and do a self-assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video self-assessment questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to answer when reviewing your submitted video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) What part of your video is the strongest? Why? Is it connected to style or content? 2) What part is the weakest — is it a problem with point of view? The content? Did you forget what you were saying? Describe. 3) What goals are you setting for your next performance?

rubrics_metrics.name: After-performance reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection questions to complete after an in-class performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Describe a moment during your performance where you felt like you were doing 'good.' What did it feel like? How did you know you were successful? What part of your material were you talking about? 2) Describe a moment during your performance where you felt unsuccessful. What did it feel like? How did you know it wasn't going well? What was missing? What could be added?

rubrics_metrics.name: In-class performance protocol — audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience Expectations: We will be kind, generous and attentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets behavioral norms for peer feedback and classroom environment during performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-class performance protocol — feedback dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback categories to be used by peers/audience during performance feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1. Material and Structure of the Joke; 2. Stage Presence and Style; 3. Performer Questions. Use these categories when giving constructive feedback.
